intro: The first subject for an Astronaut Candidate (ASCAN) is to grasp, in the language of observation, which orbit they are in and between which spacecraft and celestial bodies they will operate. The approximately two-year curriculum leads from the ISS and the Moon to Mars and beyond.
lessons.0.title: The real work begins after selection
lessons.0.summary: Selection is merely a ticket of entry. The evaluation period at Johnson Space Center determines whether one becomes an astronaut.
lessons.0.body.0: Official NASA explanations state that selected applicants are designated as Astronaut Candidates (ASCANs) and assigned to the Astronaut Office in Houston. The basic curriculum consists of approximately two years of training and evaluation; only upon fulfilling this period are they certified as astronauts. The 2025 class was officially announced as the 24th class reporting to Johnson, preparing for low Earth orbit, the Moon under Artemis, and missions beyond.
lessons.0.body.1: The curriculum is not about memorizing academic subjects. Robotics, land and water survival, geology, foreign languages, space medicine, simulated extravehicular activities, and flight in high-performance jets run in parallel. Candidates work shifts in Johnson's control room, experiencing a day in the life of those who monitor the mission.
lessons.0.body.2: This orientation is time to internalize the map for subsequent subjects. View Earth, the ISS, the Moon, and the Sun not as 'scenery,' but as operational constraints. The mini-game's orbital scan is the first observational training.
lessons.0.facts.0.label: Base
lessons.0.facts.1.label: Duration
lessons.0.facts.1.value: Approximately 2 years of training and evaluation
lessons.0.deepDive.title: What is the difference between candidate training and mission-specific training?
lessons.0.deepDive.body.0: The purpose of the basic curriculum is to build common operational capabilities among candidates with diverse professional backgrounds. Viewing this stage as the point where candidates learn to understand systems, report observations, and execute procedures as a team clarifies why flight, underwater, and geology training are part of a single curriculum.
lessons.0.deepDive.body.1: The nine subjects in this game are restructured from public materials to facilitate learning. They do not replicate the actual curriculum's sequence, evaluation criteria, or training hours. Completion of the basic curriculum and assignment to a specific spacecraft, role, or mission are separate stages.
lessons.1.title: The 2-year curriculum spans 9 operational fields
lessons.1.summary: Systems, physical fitness, spacesuits, robotics, flight, emergencies, geology, and control. A spacecraft cannot operate on just one of these.
lessons.1.body.0: Official candidate profiles list robotics, survival, geology, language, space medicine, simulated extravehicular activity (EVA), and high-performance jet training as skills for the complex operations of the ISS, Artemis lunar missions, and beyond. Summer reports add altitude chambers, emergency procedures, maintenance and repair, and cross-cultural training to this list.
lessons.1.body.1: This Academy divides the same framework into nine modules. After orientation, ISS systems and medicine open the curriculum; EVA and robotics teach life outside the vehicle and robotic arms; the T-38 and emergency modules sharpen judgment; lunar geology cultivates a scientist's perspective; and finally, the control room compresses everything into a single, unified operation.
lessons.1.body.2: Dependencies exist. Robotics and emergency modules require prior knowledge of the ISS. Lunar geology is placed after EVA to build on bodily sensation. The control room comprehensive exercise opens only after all subjects are completed. Skipping modules to pass is not permitted in actual operations.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: 2025 Class Graduation
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Destinations
lessons.2.title: Low Earth Orbit is the gateway to 'space,' yet still part of Earth
lessons.2.summary: The ISS orbits in the thin upper atmosphere, but Earth's gravity, magnetic field, and weather continue to exert influence.
lessons.2.body.0: NASA's Earth science program treats this planet as an observation target, using the ISS as one of its observation platforms. The orbital altitude is approximately 400 kilometers; while distant from the surface, it is just outside Earth compared to the distances required to reach the Moon or other planets. Residual atmosphere creates drag, causing altitude to decrease without periodic reboosts.
lessons.2.body.1: The Earth seen by the crew features weather patterns, city lights at night, and the terminator (the boundary between day and night). With an orbital period of about 90 minutes, the crew experiences approximately 16 sunrises and sunsets per day. This disrupts the circadian rhythm, which is synchronized with the 24-hour clock on the ground. In-cabin lighting and sleep schedules are used to mitigate this conflict.
lessons.2.body.2: The orientation scan first identifies the blue atmospheric rim of Earth, the sun glint on the ocean surface, and the lights on the night side. These are not merely scenic views; they are cues that inform attitude control, power management, thermal regulation, and observation window operations.
lessons.2.facts.0.label: Orbital Period
lessons.2.facts.1.label: Sunrises/Sunsets
lessons.3.title: The ISS is a laboratory, a port, and a home
lessons.3.summary: The International Space Station is a vessel in which modules from various nations are connected by a single life support and power grid.
lessons.3.body.0: Official station descriptions position the ISS as a continuously crewed research laboratory and a hub assembled and operated by international partners. Since the first module in 1998, elements from the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada have been joined, with crews living there in continuous rotation.
lessons.3.body.1: The first thing candidates should memorize is not the nicknames. They must grasp in three dimensions which modules carry the main lines for power, heat, water, and air, which are for experiments, which are airlocks, and which serve as the robot's eyes. The next subject, 'ISS Systems,' breaks this down.
lessons.3.body.2: As a port in orbit, resupply ships approach, the Canadian Arm 2 grasps them, and trusses and solar arrays generate power. In orientation, you first identify external components—solar array wings, radiators, the Cupola, Destiny, and the arm—via scanning.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Assembly Start
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Role
lessons.4.title: Living on Power and Heat During the 90-Minute Half in Shadow
lessons.4.summary: Solar arrays generate power on the day side, while the night side relies on batteries. Heat must be rejected, or the interior cannot be sustained.
lessons.4.body.0: The ISS periodically enters Earth's shadow. Power generated by the solar array wings is stored in batteries, which support life support, experiments, and communications on the night side. This is why scan training makes solar arrays one of the first targets. The wings' orientation tracks the sun. If attitude is lost, power generation drops, making the next night side difficult.
lessons.4.body.1: Heat inside the ship must be rejected, or it will accumulate. As a concept used in official scan explanations, heat is transferred from water cooling loops to ammonia outside the ship, and large radiators radiate it into space. Radiators are not merely 'cooling plates' but the exit for a closed thermal control system.
lessons.4.body.2: The transition between day and night also changes camera and eye adaptation, as well as the operation of sun sensors. At the terminator, Earth changes from daytime clouds to nighttime cities. The shutters of observation windows and the exposure of external cameras are planned with this boundary in mind.
lessons.4.facts.0.label: Day Side
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Night Side
lessons.5.title: The Moon Is the Next Site and Still a Neighbor in Orbit
lessons.5.summary: The Moon seen from the ISS is the same celestial body that Artemis will send humans to. Calibrate your sense of distance here.
lessons.5.body.0: NASA’s lunar science treats the Moon as a neighbor that preserves Earth’s history. The disk visible from the ISS window is approximately 380,000 kilometers away. This is orders of magnitude different from the 400 kilometers of low Earth orbit. Communication delays, resupply intervals, and emergency return times mean that the norms of low Earth orbit do not apply on the lunar surface.
lessons.5.body.1: Official announcements from the 2025 class explicitly state that the curriculum prepares for the ISS, the Moon via Artemis, and beyond. Field training in geology is introduced early to prepare candidates to become 'rock observers' on the Moon. In this module, we first place the position and phase of the empty Moon within the relationship between Earth and the Sun.
lessons.5.body.2: In the scan, treat the Moon as a single target. The bright highlands and dark maria will become rock names in later geology modules. For now, the first step is being able to state which side is illuminated by the Sun.
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Sense of Distance
lessons.5.facts.1.label: Next Mission
lessons.6.title: The Sun is both illumination and the source of space weather
lessons.6.summary: Power generation, heat, radiation, and communication are all driven simultaneously by the activity of the same star.
lessons.6.body.0: NASA’s solar science treats the Sun not only as a star but as a source that changes the environment of Earth and spacecraft. Flares and coronal mass ejections eject high-energy particles and magnetic disturbances. While the ISS in low orbit is protected by Earth’s magnetic field, the cancellation of extravehicular activities, sensor noise, and communication interference are real operational concerns.
lessons.6.body.1: The Sun is simultaneously the fuel for solar cells, the load on radiators, and the glare in the windows. A spacecraft’s attitude must simultaneously satisfy sun-pointing, Earth-pointing observations, and communication antenna line-of-sight. Maximizing one system compromises another.
lessons.6.body.2: Candidates should not just 'look at the Sun' but ask which aspect of current space weather constrains EVA, power, or medical operations. On the lunar surface and in deep space, the magnetic shield is thinner. Treating the Sun as an independent target in orientation is a foreshadowing of later radiation modules.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Benefit
lessons.6.facts.1.label: Threat
lessons.7.title: Observation is the technology of converting what is seen into operational data
lessons.7.summary: Gazing out the window and identifying targets to record facts are distinct skills.
lessons.7.body.0: The orbital scan mini-game requires you to identify the solar arrays, radiators, cupola, Destiny module, Canadarm2, the terminator, city lights at night, the atmospheric limb, and ocean glint in sequence. You must pick out the targets repeatedly shown in official station and Earth observation footage within a time limit.
lessons.7.body.1: A good scan does not end with just naming the object. You must capture its function in a single sentence, such as 'Solar arrays are the power input,' 'Radiators are the heat output,' or 'The cupola is the arm's eyes.' A report that can be handed to CAPCOM on the ground is the completed form of observation.
lessons.7.body.2: Incorrect targets are added to a review list. Astronaut training follows the same principle: do not hide misidentifications, but correct them in the next orbit. The orbit returns in 90 minutes. The next chance comes only to those who are prepared.
lessons.7.facts.0.label: Targets
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Outcome
lessons.8.title: International cooperation is not a matter of etiquette, but a prerequisite for operations
lessons.8.summary: Modules, languages, and procedures cannot be completed by a single nation. This is why Russian language and cross-cultural training are included in the candidate curriculum.
lessons.8.body.0: The ISS was assembled through a partnership including NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, and CSA. Official candidate articles state that intensive Russian language and cross-cultural training is conducted to prepare for missions that cross national borders. The displays on the other side of the hatch and emergency communications cannot be handled in English alone.
lessons.8.body.1: Official records of JAXA astronauts accompanying geological training in Iceland are an example of how scientific language is shared across borders. Robotics relies on the Canadian arm, experiments on Japanese and European modules, and propulsion and part of the habitat on the Russian segment. In the event of a failure, choosing the wrong partner's procedure manual will cause time to be lost.
lessons.8.body.2: During orientation, do not end the discussion of nationality with mere emotion. Hold a map of whose module, whose communication network, and whose recovery team will be involved. This forms the foundation for subsequent emergency and control subjects.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Languages
lessons.8.facts.1.label: Skills
lessons.8.facts.1.value: Sharing procedures in a cross-cultural context
lessons.9.title: Move on to the next subject with a record of your weaknesses
lessons.9.summary: Passing orientation does not mean knowing everything, but being able to state what needs to be deepened next.
lessons.9.body.0: The official curriculum is also an evaluation period. The 2011 explanation notes that final astronaut certification depends on the successful completion of training and evaluation. The quizzes and scans in this module are designed to visualize gaps in knowledge.
lessons.9.body.1: Earth's day and night, the ISS's external components, the Moon's distance, and the Sun's duality. If you can explain these in operational terms, you can break down the internal water, air, and power systems in the next ISS module. If you cannot, you will get lost in memorizing module names.
lessons.9.body.2: The 'ASCAN Enlistment' badge is a mark of departure. The mark of arrival is not awarded until the final integrated control exercise. Take the map and descend to the next site.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: This Module
lessons.9.facts.1.label: Next
quiz.0.prompt: What is the term used by NASA's official explanation for candidates after selection?
quiz.0.explanation: Selected candidates are called Astronaut Candidates and undergo approximately two years of training and evaluation at Johnson's Astronaut Office.
quiz.1.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the position of the candidate program as indicated by the official explanation?
quiz.1.choices.1: A period of training and evaluation, after which one becomes an astronaut only upon successful completion
quiz.1.choices.3: Qualification for remote operation of unmanned aircraft only
quiz.1.explanation: It is officially stated that final astronaut certification depends on the successful completion of the training and evaluation period.
quiz.2.prompt: What value is used in this module and the scan materials as a guideline for the time it takes the ISS to orbit Earth once?
quiz.2.explanation: The ISS orbits Earth in approximately 90 minutes, resulting in about 16 sunrises and sunsets per day.
quiz.3.prompt: As a result of the approximately 90-minute orbital period, what is the approximate number of sunrises and sunsets the crew experiences per day?
quiz.3.explanation: The 90-minute period results in approximately 16 day-night cycles per 24 hours. Sleep and lighting schedules are necessary.
quiz.4.prompt: Which year is officially cited as the start of ISS assembly?
quiz.4.explanation: Following the first module, international partners continued to add modules, creating a continuous crewed research station. 1998 is the start of assembly.
quiz.5.prompt: While the ISS is in Earth's shadow, what primarily supports its power supply?
quiz.5.choices.3: Power transmission from a lunar base
quiz.5.explanation: Power collected by the solar arrays is stored in batteries, which support life support, experiments, and communications on the night side.
quiz.6.prompt: Which device does the scan material identify for rejecting excess heat from the cabin into space?
quiz.6.explanation: Heat is transferred from the water loop to ammonia outside the spacecraft and radiated into space via large radiators.
quiz.7.prompt: What target does the official announcement for the 2025 candidate class list as a milestone of training?
quiz.7.choices.1: Reproduction of the Apollo program only
quiz.7.choices.3: ISS, Artemis lunar missions, and beyond
quiz.7.explanation: The official announcement states that the curriculum prepares candidates for low Earth orbit, Artemis lunar missions, and beyond.
quiz.8.prompt: Which is an appropriate potential impact of solar activity on ISS operations?
quiz.8.choices.0: Cancellation of EVAs or disruption of communications and sensors
quiz.8.explanation: Flares and particle radiation can affect EVA decisions, sensors, and communications. The Sun is simultaneously a power source and a source of space weather.
quiz.9.prompt: What training does the official summer report state candidates are undergoing to prepare for international missions?
quiz.9.explanation: Candidates undergo intensive Russian language and cross-cultural training while concurrently learning spacecraft systems, EVA, and emergency procedures.
quiz.10.prompt: What does this lesson require as the outcome of a good orbital scan?
quiz.10.choices.2: Recording the function in one sentence in addition to the name
quiz.10.explanation: Identification becomes operational data only when it includes function. A one-sentence description that can be passed to CAPCOM is the complete form of observation.
quiz.11.prompt: What graduation timing for the 2025 class does the official summer report indicate?
quiz.11.explanation: The official article states that the class is on track for graduation in 2027.
quiz.12.prompt: When describing the ISS in one word, which three roles does this lesson emphasize?
quiz.12.explanation: It is a port where the crew lives, conducts experiments, and receives resupply ships. Identifying external components is also a training exercise in understanding its function as a port.
quiz.13.prompt: Regarding the sense of distance between low Earth orbit and the Moon, which of the following does this lesson correct?
quiz.13.choices.0: The Moon is at the same altitude as the ISS
quiz.13.choices.1: The Moon is orders of magnitude farther than LEO, changing the time required for return and communication
quiz.13.choices.2: The Moon is closer than the Sun, so it is safe
quiz.13.choices.3: On the lunar surface, one can orbit the Earth in 90 minutes
quiz.13.explanation: The distance to the Moon is on the scale of approximately one thousand times the altitude of low Earth orbit, changing the norms for emergency return and resupply.
quiz.14.prompt: Which control-side experience does the official article state that candidates are made to experience?
quiz.14.choices.2: Working a shift in the Houston control room
quiz.14.explanation: Astronaut Candidates Get to Work states that candidates work shifts at the MCC and experience the day of the people who watch over them.
quiz.15.prompt: What does this lesson set as a passing condition for orientation?
quiz.15.choices.0: A PhD in all space sciences
quiz.15.choices.3: Being able to state the next weakness to improve
quiz.15.explanation: This subject provides a map and observation patterns. Certification comes after the entire course; for now, the goal is to visualize gaps and move forward.
glossary.0.description: Personnel who, after selection, undergo approximately two years of training and evaluation at Johnson, and become astronauts upon meeting the requirements.
glossary.1.description: The altitude band in which the ISS orbits. Atmospheric drag and the Earth's magnetic field still have an effect, and it takes about 90 minutes to complete one orbit.
glossary.2.description: The boundary line between day and night on Earth. From the ISS window, it appears as a moving band of light and shadow.
glossary.3.description: The phenomenon where the sea surface reflects sunlight like a mirror. It highlights differences in the state of the water surface.
glossary.4.description: A crewed research facility operated by international partners. It serves as a residence, laboratory, and port for resupply ships.
glossary.5.description: Particle streams and magnetic disturbances caused by solar activity. It can affect EVAs, communications, sensors, and radiation exposure.
glossary.6.description: The core hub for human spaceflight located in Houston. Candidate training, mission control, the NBL, and flight operations are concentrated here.
glossary.7.description: NASA's program to resume crewed lunar exploration. The candidate course prepares for this lunar mission in addition to the ISS.
